item.title: Kash Doll Puts Detroit Thanksgiving Giveaway Under Her Own Foundation
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Kash Doll brings DTLR into her first Fairy Boss Muva Foundation giveaway, a new chapter in her Detroit holiday work.
item.content:encoded:
Kash Doll put her own foundation behind a Detroit Thanksgiving giveaway for the first time. Fairy Boss Muva teamed up with sneaker retailer DTLR for a November 21 food distribution at its Belmont Plaza store on East Eight Mile Road.

The Detroit rapper said she’d been doing giveaways for more than a decade, but Saturday’s event was the first she billed as a Fairy Boss Muva Foundation giveaway.

“This year feels extra special because it’s my first official giveaway under my foundation, Fairy Boss Muva,” Kash Doll wrote on X.

The local event listing put the giveaway from 1 to 4 p.m. and said the turkeys and fresh produce would be free while supplies lasted. Kash Doll invited families to bring their children and spend time together.

Detroit has seen Kash Doll pitch in before. She and Icewear Vezzo helped distribute food at Hart Plaza in 2019, when volunteers handed out 2,000 turkeys at a Heartsgiving food drive led by Vezzo’s Detroit Rappers Organization. Detroit’s City Council also lists Kash Doll among the artists who’ve attended kickoffs for Occupy the Corner, a summer program that connects residents with food, health care and job resources.

Kash Doll has also helped Detroiters pay for career training. Four students received phlebotomy scholarships through her 2018 Christmas giveaway after applicants wrote essays explaining why they needed the help. She gave out 20 vocational health care scholarships the following year with the Detroit Health Department and Phlebotomy Express Training.

In an interview with REVOLT about her community work, Kash Doll explained why she kept coming back. “Detroit is one of those cities that you have to water. You have to water where you’re from anyway, I believe,” she said.

The city is part of Kash Doll’s music, too. She wrote rhymes and practiced freestyling on the way to school, and she was still getting hometown welcomes years after breaking out, including when Trey Songz brought her out during his Detroit tour stop.

Kash Doll’s earlier work in the city also included B.A.D. Girls, an initiative that helped young women get to prom with dresses and styling.

item.title: Meek Mill Points Listeners To His Own App For Music And Podcasts
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Meek Mill wants a direct line to listeners, and he's bringing plans for new music and podcasts to his DC Club app.
item.content:encoded:
Meek Mill is steering listeners to DC Club, his own fan app, with plans to stream podcasts and put out new music there. He’s asking listeners to come straight to him instead of hunting for his next release across several different services.

Meek pointed people to the app on X on Sunday, November 22. He pushed back on the expectation that artists should put out music on the same Friday schedule, then told followers, “come to the dc club we will stream podcast drop new music,” he wrote.

Meek said he also plans to give away prizes and talk with supporters through DC Club. In a November 20 post linking to the same app, he explained why he wanted another way to reach them: “it’s been hard to access the fans so I started building my own world!”

Meek had already talked about the shift from mixtapes to streaming in an interview on On Wax With Lyor Cohen. The discussion covered what changed as algorithms started shaping how listeners find songs and how Meek has used new technology in his own work.

The App Store listing shows DC Club is free to download on iPhone and iPad, with some content available without paying. Its monthly Premium subscription offers unreleased music, members-only releases, a group chat and early access to concert tickets. Listeners can also get updates from Meek and browse a shop for his and Dream Chasers’ merchandise.

The pitch follows Meek’s public push for artists to run their own platforms. Meek raised the idea after Doe Boy brought up how sites like LiveMixtapes and Spinrilla helped people find new rappers. Meek’s argument was that getting on a big playlist was difficult, and strong streaming numbers didn’t guarantee artists would get paid by their labels.

The Dream Chasers name goes back to his mixtape years, including Dreamchasers 2 in 2012. It also appears on his recent independent releases, including Indie Pack (Vol. 01), which lists DreamChasers as the label and Stem as the distributor. The four-track EP includes “4TH OF JULY” with fellow Philadelphia artist Fridayy.

Apple’s version history shows DC Club was already getting updates when version 1.0.32 appeared on November 3.

item.title: Will Smith’s Calabasas Property Hit By Early-Morning Fire
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Authorities confirm a fire on Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's Calabasas property is out after crews responded Monday.
item.content:encoded:
Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith’s Calabasas property was the scene of an early-morning fire Monday, November 23. The fire broke out in a shack on the property, and the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department confirmed it was extinguished, according to Page Six.

Footage obtained by Page Six showed emergency vehicles arriving in the dark as smoke rose from the property. It was not clear whether the flames reached the main house.

The cause of the fire and the extent of the damage were not immediately reported. There was no confirmation that either Smith was at the property. A representative for Will Smith did not immediately respond to Page Six’s request for comment.

Another fire broke out at the property in September 2021. That one started in the basement and led to renovations, Page Six reported. AllHipHop covered the emergency response at the time, including reports that the home sustained smoke damage.

The property was also near the path of the 2018 Woolsey Fire. Smith told Instagram followers he went outside to look after his daughter Willow grew worried. “We’re probably about eight miles away from it,” he said in a video quoted by Page Six.

The Woolsey Fire burned nearly 97,000 acres across Los Angeles and Ventura counties, according to Cal Fire.

item.title: KRS-One’s Temple Of Hip Hop Opens Its Doors For Newark’s Turkey Giveaway
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: KRS-One's Newark Temple becomes a Thanksgiving pickup spot as the city offers free turkeys to residents with valid ID.
item.content:encoded:
KRS-One‘s Temple of Hip Hop is where Newark plans to hand out free Thanksgiving turkeys Monday, November 23. The city’s annual giveaway runs from noon to 6 p.m. at 55 Ludlow Street in the South Ward, where the Boogie Down Productions MC built a home for Hip-Hop classes and community events.

The giveaway is open only to Newark residents, the mayor’s office announced. Residents need a valid ID, and the city will hand out turkeys on a first-come basis while supplies last. The office also encourages people to contact their ward’s mayoral aide in advance to reserve a turkey.

Newark has used the building for Thanksgiving before. In 2023, the city and its partners handed out 3,600 Thanksgiving dinners at the same address, according to partner Table to Table.

KRS-One told Talib Kweli and Tef Poe in an interview on Lemme Ask You This that the city holds its own events there alongside the Temple’s courses and classes, as part of its partnership with the center.

“So the city has its own events that it throws at the Temple of Hip Hop as well,” KRS-One said.

On January 7, 2026, the Municipal Council approved an agreement by an 8-0 vote to give the Krist Foundation space at the city’s Training Recreation Education Center on Ludlow Street. The plan calls for instruction in beatboxing, songwriting and audio engineering for people 16 and older, including people who live outside the city.

Under the agreement, Newark residents 16 and older can take the classes for free with the city’s recreation department Community Pass Card. Participants can earn certificates in their areas of study. The foundation also plans to work with people in music and entertainment to help students find internships or jobs.

The Temple traces its roots to the Stop the Violence Movement and 1989’s “Self-Destruction,” when KRS-One and other rappers got on one record to confront violence in their communities. In 2024, he was set to lead a Bronx march for health and peaceful conflict resolution, with a free concert planned at the Newark Temple later that day.

Anyone with questions about Monday’s distribution can call Newark’s Special Projects office at 973-733-5460.

item.title: Don Toliver’s Manchester Concert Evacuated, One Person Taken To Hospital
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Police escort more than 12,000 people out of Don Toliver's Manchester show after reports of an unknown substance.
item.content:encoded:
Don Toliver‘s Manchester concert ended early on Sunday (November 22), and one person was taken to hospital after people in the crowd reported feeling the effects of an unknown substance.

Greater Manchester Police said more than 12,000 people were safely escorted out of Co-op Live.

Venue staff alerted police shortly after 10 p.m. Officers responded with other emergency crews, and police declared a major incident so the different agencies could work together.

“Several people were treated on site, and one has been taken to hospital at this time,” Greater Manchester Police Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said.

North West Ambulance Service said its clinicians assessed more than 50 people, some with eye or breathing symptoms, according to The Guardian.

The service said crews were carrying out decontamination as a precaution and took one patient to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment.

Its response included a team trained to treat patients in hazardous areas.

Police initially said they believed the substance was tear gas.

In their follow-up, they called it an unknown substance and said they were investigating what it was and what caused the incident.

Co-op Live said in a statement that it was working with police to determine what happened at the arena.

Police advised anyone who started feeling ill after leaving the concert to go to their local hospital.

The Manchester date was part of the second leg of Toliver’s world tour. Co-op Live billed the show as his return to the arena during his run across Europe and the United Kingdom.

Toliver’s tour had a separate interruption at Houston’s Toyota Center in August.

The Houston Chronicle footage below shows that earlier show ending with an announcement for the crowd to leave after a man allegedly brought a gun into the venue.

AllHipHop reported that Toyota Center officials and Atlantic Records cited safety concerns when they called off the rest of the Houston concert.

Toliver’s next scheduled dates were at The O2 in London on November 23 and OVO Arena Wembley on November 24.

item.title: David Banner Calls Out Rapper Podcasts: “Ain’t Nobody Talking About Sh*t”
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: David Banner tells Chuck “Jigsaw” Creekmur what he thinks is missing from rapper podcasts.
item.content:encoded:
David Banner does not hold back. The brother is dope on the mic, dope on the beats, and he can act. And when he gets going on something he cares about, you might as well put the phone down and listen. He’s a friend of the site and the founders, too. So before we get into it, go check out “Where You From?” with T.I., Juicy J and Duke Deuce. That’s a whole Southern lineup right there. It’s hot in the streets and the streams!

Now, Banner sat down with the Media GOAT Chuck “Jigsaw” Creekmur for AllHipHop, and that interview went all over the place in the best way. They talked about new music, the people he’s working with and what it can cost to speak freely. Then they got to rappers and their podcasts. You already know Banner had something to say about that. 

“Think about this. I never said this before. Think about all the f**king podcasts we have now. Just every rapper has a podcast. This is the least amount of information that has been disseminated amongst people, and we got more microphones in front of us and ain’t nobody talking about sh*t. We ain’t learn nothing about African culture. We ain’t learn nothing about Indigenous people. We ain’t learned about nothing that’s going on in politics. None of this shit! And we have all the mics that we control and we choose not to say nothing?”

Jigsaw was just going “Mhm” and whistling. I get it. I like a good rap story as much as anybody. But if you’ve got your own show and people are already tuning in, what else could you get them talking about? Banner put three subjects on the table before Jigsaw could get another word in.

Banner’s been doing this since his days inJackson, Mississippi. In 2003, Mississippi: The Album gave us “Like a Pimp” with Lil’ Flip and “Cadillac on 22’s,” where Banner brought up the death of Andre Jones in a Mississippi jail. His nonprofit, Heal the Hood, helped people affected by Hurricane Katrina. In 2007, he testified before Congress, arguing that rap reflected problems already present in American communities. So when Banner asks what rappers are doing with their microphones, remember what he did with his when the whole country was listening. 

READ ALSO: David Banner Opens Up About Therapy, Burnout & Nearly Quitting Rap!

What do y’all think? Is Banner right about rapper podcasts? Drop your thoughts in the comments and tell us who you think is using their mic well.

item.title: E.D.I. Mean Explains Why He Won’t Perform Tupac’s “Hit ‘Em Up” Again
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: E.D.I. Mean says he and Young Noble agreed to stop performing Tupac's 1996 diss track, even though crowds still ask for it.
item.content:encoded:
E.D.I. Mean says he’s done performing Tupac Shakur’s “Hit ‘Em Up.”

The Outlawz rapper told Drink Champs that he and Young Noble agreed to drop the diss track from their live shows before Noble died.

“Before my brother Noble died, we was like, yo, we’re not doing ‘Hit ‘Em Up’ no more,” he told N.O.R.E. and DJ EFN. Mean said that decision was about the stage.

He had no problem with fans continuing to play the record.

E.D.I. Mean knows crowds still ask for the song, but he drew a firm line about doing his verse again: “I’m not rapping that shit.”

He said he was 21 when he took part in the diss and didn’t feel the same way about rapping it 30 years later.

E.D.I. Mean also said he still talks to Lil Cease, who performed with The Notorious B.I.G. in Junior M.A.F.I.A. That relationship came up when the hosts asked what it was like to record a diss aimed at people he respected.

E.D.I. Mean remembers the song being hard to leave off the setlist. Audiences would listen to the other songs but still wait to hear “Hit ‘Em Up,” he said. He had talked about its effect on crowds before and said fights had broken out at shows when he performed it.

Shakur released the record in 1996 with the Outlawz, taking aim at Biggie and Bad Boy Records.

The track came out on the same single as “How Do U Want It,” his collaboration with K-Ci and JoJo.

E.D.I. Mean continued working alongside Noble after Shakur’s death. He announced Noble’s death in July 2025.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Chronic Law Gets Hearing On Two Bids To Block Evidence In Federal Gun Case
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Chronic Law gets a December court date in Georgia to challenge the car search and FBI questioning behind his gun case.
item.content:encoded:
Chronic Law will appear in federal court on two separate attempts to keep evidence out of his Georgia gun case.

A judge set both challenges for December 9, giving his lawyers a chance to contest what deputies found in a car and what the dancehall artist later told the FBI.

U.S. District Judge W. Louis Sands signed the order and set the hearing for 11 A.M. at the C.B. King United States Courthouse in Albany, Georgia. He hasn’t decided whether the government can use either set of evidence.

The first challenge goes back to a November 15, 2025, traffic stop in Turner County, Georgia. Federal prosecutors say deputies tried to pull Chronic Law over for speeding, then found four guns after the car stopped.

Defense attorney Ana Davide argues that deputies searched the car without a warrant and found the firearms before a police dog did.

Prosecutor Shiante McMahon says officers were taking inventory before towing the car and argues the dog’s alert gave them a separate reason to search.

Davide’s second motion targets statements Chronic Law made to FBI Special Agent Andrew Nelson.

She argues that Nelson asked “express questions” that she says were likely to draw incriminating answers during two arrests without getting a valid waiver of his Miranda rights.

Federal prosecutors say Chronic Law told agents the firearms were his.

The defense wants that statement kept out of trial, along with any evidence it led investigators to, and Sands expects written arguments to wrap up by December 3.

Chronic Law was arrested in Miami in July on a federal charge of possessing a firearm as a prohibited person. He pleaded not guilty in Georgia and is being held before trial.

Chronic Law has worked with New York artists on both sides of the rap-and-dancehall divide. He joined Kranium on “Higher Life” and collaborated with French Montana on the “NY Girls” remix with CJTheChemist.

The court previously moved Chronic Law’s trial to its January 2027 term.

item.title: Brandy Wants ‘Moesha’ Back After Helping Revive ‘A Different World’
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Brandy sees a way back for Moesha after singing the theme for Netflix's A Different World sequel and reuniting with Usher.
item.content:encoded:
Brandy wants another shot at Moesha, and she has a recent example of how a return could work.

The R&B singer pointed to Netflix’s A Different World sequel, a show that brought her in to record its new theme song.

“Moesha can really be something in today’s time, especially since we’ve seen the success of A Different World,” Brandy said in an interview on The Jennifer Hudson Show.

Brandy played Moesha Mitchell from 1996 to 2001. The UPN sitcom followed a Los Angeles teenager as she navigated school, romance and a changing family.

Brandy told Hudson that she sees Moesha differently now than she did when she was younger and has grown to appreciate the character’s choices.

The show also gave Brandy a screen partner in Usher, who played her love interest.

The two shared a stage again at SoFi Stadium in September, when he brought her out during his tour with Chris Brown. Brandy performed “Top of the World” and “I Wanna Be Down.”

She told Hudson they used to challenge each other to sing on the Moesha set.

The comparison to A Different World comes from experience.

Netflix brought Brandy in to put her stamp on the song longtime viewers knew in Aretha Franklin’s voice. The new recording keeps the original lyrics.

“It also inspired me to want to do more acting. Just seeing people that looked like me on television made me dream bigger,” Brandy told Netflix’s Tudum about the original series.

The sequel follows Deborah Wayne, the daughter of Dwayne and Whitley, back to Hillman College.

The sequel drew 4.2 million views in its first week after its September 24 premiere and debuted at No. 4 on Netflix’s English TV chart. Netflix has renewed it for a second season.

Brandy talked about revisiting Moesha in 2020, after the original series arrived on Netflix. The singer said at the time that she had begun talking to people who could help make it happen.

item.title: Skepta Sweeps The Top Four Spots On The Official UK Rap Chart
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Skepta claims all four top spots on the Official UK Rap Chart, led by Broken Hearts with Central Cee and Jorja Smith.
item.content:encoded:
Skepta went from holding the top three spots on the Official UK Rap Chart to taking all four.

“Broken Hearts,” his collaboration with Central Cee and Jorja Smith, moved to No. 1 on the November 20 chart. “Currency” followed at No. 2, Fakemink’s “Chiltern Firehouse” featuring Skepta jumped from No. 6 to No. 3, and Skepta’s solo track “Revenge” entered at No. 4.

It’s the first time an artist has had a credit on all four leading records in the chart’s three editions.

D-Block Europe and Young Adz took the inaugural No. 1 with “What U Wanna Do,” while Skepta and Fakemink started at No. 2.

On the November 13 chart, Skepta led with “Currency,” followed by “Broken Hearts” and “Secrets of Patriarchy.” Bexblu and Paul Stephan held No. 4 that week with “Sound of the South.”

Skepta had first tried “Broken Hearts” with Dave, he told British GQ in an interview.

Central Cee put a verse on the track, and another decision brought in Smith.

“I had a vocal from a sample pack, and we all thought it would be best to replace the sample with Jorja,” Skepta said.

Three of this week’s top four come from The Fork and Knife.

The exception is the Fakemink collaboration, which wasn’t on the 15-track album and has appeared on all three editions of the chart.

“Revenge,” meanwhile, is the newest chart entry of the four.
